newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia says heartened by Cambodian assembly vote.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia says heartened by Cambodian assembly vote.

text.p: Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi said on Thursday the election of a new premier in troubled Cambodia was a "heartening" development.

"It is heartening to note that the Cambodia National Assembly met and I haven't heard of any unruly assembly or anyone stopped from addressing the assembly," Abdullah told reporters after addressing a conference on regional issues.
"This means the existing government is functioning."
Abdullah was speaking ahead of Monday's meeting in Singapore of foreign ministers from the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) to discuss the latest developments in Cambodia.
Cambodia's ousted Prince Norodom Ranariddh on Wednesday was replaced as first prime minister by Foreign Minister Ung Huot in a move strongman Hun Sen said signalled an end to the turmoil.
Eighty-six members of the 120-seat National Assembly voted by secret ballot in favour of Ung Huot. A total of 99 assembly members attended the Wednesday session.
Second Prime Minster Hun Sen, who ousted Ranariddh in a bloody coup early last month, hailed the assembly's overwhelming approval of the man he backed for the job.

Cambodia was supposed to have joined ASEAN, along with Burma and Laos, at the grouping's annual meeting in Kuala Lumpur last month. But ASEAN has postponed Cambodia's admission indefinitely pending a resolution of the crisis.
ASEAN -- Brunei, Burma, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- has taken the lead role in efforts to find a solution to Cambodia's woes.
The Singapore meeting will hear a report by three ASEAN ministers who met Hun Sen last Saturday in Phnom Penh.

Led by Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas, and including Philippines Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon and Thai Foreign Minister Prachuab Chaiyasan, the trio is trying to mediate a solution among Cambodia's warring factions.
Malaysia's Abdullah said the meeting called by Siazon, the current ASEAN chairman, "would decide on ASEAN's future role in mediation".
Abdullah declined further comment, saying: "I don't want the ASEAN consensus to be split. Since we have an ASEAN meeting on this matter, we want it to be a united view."
Asked about Cambodia's chances for early admission to ASEAN, he said: "I can't even speculate on that. We will only know after the (three ministers') report has been reviewed."
ASEAN diplomats said the role of King Norodom Sihanouk is crucial -- he will have to decide whether to accept Ung Huot as a legitimate first premier.

Sihanouk said late last month he would not recognise Ung Huot as first premier as the post belonged to his son. The king also said that a vote on a new first prime minister by an incomplete parliament would be invalid.
Hun Sen has said he and Ung Huot would visit Sihanouk in Beijing, where the king is receiving medical treatment.
The United States and ASEAN both said after the prince's ouster that they still recognised him as first prime minister.
"The issue (at the Singapore meeting) is the election of Ung Huot and what to do about it," one ASEAN diplomat said. "The issue at the moment is not when Cambodia will join ASEAN."
